name: Gareth Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth, 58, a junior electrician after the goods-checking warehouse where I worked closed. I've a vocational certificate only, no electrician's licence, and I'm still below the experienced workers' skill level, so the senior assigns and checks tasks and signs off installations. I like finally getting a drawing to match the fittings in front of me, but tracing an unfamiliar fault still needs explaining. I use AI occasionally for a checked study explanation once a colleague has shown the method, rather than let a confident answer replace the senior's checks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What sits around the work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Milan books freight deliveries, our children are thirty and thirty-six and live elsewhere, and we still have a mortgage. My pay is typical, we have two months of expenses saved, and there are some other electrical employers nearby, but I have no offer from one. The firm gives us a rota a week at a time, and one shop postponing its repair already cost me a paid day this month. Both wages cover today's bills, but retirement is a question I haven't put confirmed figures or a stopping date against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a little useful software is fine without promising a whole new kind of worker. I'd keep using the checked study explanation when it helped. I'd also like next week's paid days written down before we had another conversation about what might happen in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the actual rota already. Two months saved gives us a buffer, but a run of postponed repairs would reduce the wage our mortgage needs. Milan's freight-booking pay carries on much as before in this picture, so the uncertainty isn't something I need to blame on a new AI announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep a paper record of confirmed paid days and cancelled jobs, asking the manager each Thursday what the following week actually guaranteed. Through the next year I'd keep supervised electrical work and occasional checked study notes, not count an unoffered shift as pay. Milan and I would keep the existing budget and reserve, entering no retirement payment before its actual amount and date were confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some relief that the trade doesn't change its whole shape. I can deal with a wrong fitting more easily than a paid day that vanishes by phone. The reserve means we can ask a careful question instead of make a panic promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when a job was postponed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark it as money not earned and ask whether another paid supervised task was actually available. I wouldn't enter a possible replacement call in the household total until it was confirmed. A pencil can leave a space in the diary without filling the bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to check about retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want actual amounts, dates and conditions beside our real mortgage and essential costs. I wouldn't copy another person's stopping birthday or count our grown children's wages. Two saved months isn't an answer about how to fund the years after work.

I'd ask for **next week's paid days** before another broad discussion of the distant future.
think: My **rota uncertainty** already threatens the wage if postponed repairs continue.
Two months saved provides a **short buffer**, while Milan's wage continues here without removing the need for mine.
do: Record **confirmed paid days** and cancellations, checking next week's guarantee with the manager each Thursday.
Keep **supervised work** and occasional checked study notes, counting no unoffered shift as income.
Retain the **existing budget and reserve**, entering no retirement payment before actual amount and date are confirmed.
feel: **Anxious about paid days**, with enough buffer to check terms carefully rather than make an immediate panic promise.

His **certificate-only competence** stays junior and supervised, with occasional checked AI study distinguished from installation approval or routine autonomous work.

steps.text: Keep supervised electrical work and check confirmed paid days every Thursday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the manager booking and freight paperwork are thinking tasks even when my fittings still need hands. Milan's paid desk work belongs in that conversation too. I'd try a proven new tool, but it needs to earn a place without taking paid checking out of the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior hours could shrink if faster planning leaves fewer paid days for learners. Milan's bookings and customer calls could also move to software, so both wages have a reason to worry us. Two months saved gives some control, not a reason to call either wage optional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the colleague who tested the approved AI drawing-label aid to show six completed examples. In the first year I'd learn it only free inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained, and require the senior to check each suggested label before real use. I'd keep supervised work and the Thursday paid-days check, budgeting only actual agreed wages from both jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the money, and interested in whether a clear demonstration would stop me getting the drawing wrong. I'd rather ask what the tool missed than use it to look confident. A new screen doesn't know which paid day the mortgage was waiting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the suggested label was wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop that example and show the senior the drawing beside the suggestion. I wouldn't use a guessed label on the actual task. The approval still belongs with the qualified person checking the work, not the phone that suggested a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if practice cost a fee or unpaid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the old approved method and ask for a free demonstration inside paid hours later. I wouldn't pay a personal fee or lose normal weekly wages to look willing. The household needs the wage before I can celebrate the time saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work thinking AGI arrives in 2028, with capable robots around 2031 for the physical tasks. Milan's booking wage faces the earlier date, while I'd be 60 and then 63. I'd ask for actual income choices rather than let a birthday stand in for a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Milan's booking income to go in 2028. My own paid week isn't dependable enough to cover the present mortgage and essentials alone, and fitting hours could shrink further when robots follow. Two months saved isn't a confirmed bridge to any retirement income, and I'd be losing sleep over that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request free evening community advice, subject to availability, with both wage records, the mortgage and actual retirement papers to check real figures and dates. In 2029 I'd apply for advertised supervised electrical roles matching my actual ability, keeping the present job until signed pay terms and guaranteed hours covered mortgage, essentials and travel costs. Milan and I would agree any changed household commitments before acceptance, and we'd count neither an unconfirmed job nor an unknown retirement payment in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can still request advice and apply. I'd be frightened of the first missing booking wage while my own rota was still a week at a time. I don't want the word retired used to tidy up money that hasn't been found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a different role suitable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the actual tasks, who supervised them and the written hours and rate before leaving. I wouldn't choose an unsupervised electrical role because it had a better title. A vocational certificate isn't an electrician's licence just because the mortgage is urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no suitable signed offer existed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the actual current wage where work was offered and seek available advice using the real gap. I wouldn't borrow for an unchosen course or assume another employer would hire me at 61. Applying is something I can do; the offer isn't mine to invent.

feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, while requesting advice and applying without assuming an appointment, offer or affordable next wage.
S2.quote: Applying is something I can do; the offer isn't mine to invent.
fieldNote: His expected **household loss** begins in 2028 through booking work, with later physical exposure kept distinct rather than moving robots forward.
The **job conditions** preserve supervised suitable tasks, actual vacancies, signed affordable pay, guaranteed hours, travel costs and prior household agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us check actual figures before thinking AGI in 2031, with capable robots around 2034. I'd be 63 and then 66. I'd still want a paid job's hours written down rather than assume another qualification or another birthday supplied the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of Milan's booking income in 2031, and today's uncertain rota already makes me nervous. More time could let us check costs and a real job offer, but it doesn't tell me what income replaces the gap. I'd be losing sleep without pretending turning 63 brings a payment we haven't confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request free evening advice now, subject to availability, to check real resource amounts, dates and conditions, keeping current supervised work where offered. In 2032 I'd be 64 and would apply for advertised supervised electrical roles only if income was still needed and duties matched my actual ability. I'd leave only with signed pay terms and guaranteed hours covering mortgage, essentials and travel, with Milan agreeing actual household commitments before acceptance; no signed offer or confirmed affordable exit means no promise that the gap is solved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the expected missing wage, with more time to check one option before another. I could bring a statement back and ask what it actually paid. I'd still have to live on actual wages during the questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use a resource that started paying later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare its confirmed start date and conditions with the actual bills in each period. A later figure isn't money for this month's mortgage. Milan and I would decide from the real budget before I chose any exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the longer warning still produced no suitable vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking for suitable paid supervised work if income was needed, while saying honestly that a vacancy might not exist. I wouldn't treat a willing application as proof someone would hire me. My job is to check the opportunity, not guarantee the employer's answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years gives us room to check a real answer, not permission to assume every older worker has the same ending. Thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and capable robots around 2039. I'd keep paid work and proper checks now while we found out the resource figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 at the thinking date and about 71 when the robots followed. I don't know whether an affordable exit would exist before then, or what work I'd actually be able to do. Our current two-month cushion and typical pay still leave the weekly rota a real worry now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request free evening advice now, subject to availability, to check actual resources and costs, reviewing confirmed wages with Milan monthly, sooner if paid days changed. In 2037 I'd be 69 and would apply for real supervised electrical vacancies only if income was needed and the tasks matched my actual ability, requiring signed pay terms and guaranteed hours covering mortgage, essentials and travel before leaving any current work. We'd agree actual household commitments before acceptance, without assuming a job, a pension payment or physical work capacity because the budget wanted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present week, with less certainty of a fixed future loss ten years away. I can be glad of time without pretending it changes next Thursday's rota. I'd like enough room to read a statement without making it a prophecy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help from your grown children mean over the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what either grown child had actually offered and whether it fitted their own time and costs. They are adults already and would have their own later lives. I wouldn't count their wages or a spare room in our household budget before a conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if neither suitable paid work nor an affordable exit was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what actual resources or support could be checked against the real gap, keeping any paid work within my ability and the required supervision. I wouldn't promise to do physical tasks at 71 because I needed the money. A budget isn't evidence that a person can still do a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect Milan's booking wage to fall before our uncertain paid weeks have a confirmed replacement. Written paid hours, supervised practical work and advice giving actual resource figures and dates would help. I need a paid week I can put beside the mortgage, not another age someone tells me ought to feel reassuring.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it feels like to be asked about retirement while still learning the first part of a trade. I can see the wish to stop and the need to get better at working at the same time. I'd like the plan to notice both without pretending either one has already been paid for.

headlineQuote: I need a paid week I can put beside the mortgage, not another age someone tells me ought to feel reassuring.
portrait: Gareth, **58**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate only, still learning under senior checks after his former warehouse closed.
He has **typical pay**, two months saved and some nearby electrical employers, with freight-booking partner Milan, grown children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI occasionally** after demonstration, with a new label aid still requiring free paid practice and senior checking before actual use.
His **job search** requires suitable supervised duties, signed affordable pay, guaranteed hours, travel costs and household agreement, without assuming later hiring.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected loss of most of Milan's booking income before confirmed replacement, with later physical-hour risks adding uncertainty.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours**, supervised practical work and advice supplying actual resource figures and dates would help build a real budget.
